extracted.intended_audience: DHS adjudicators, immigration attorneys/practitioners, visa applicants and petitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and procedures DHS will apply to determine whether an alien is likely to become a public charge (including factors to weigh, evidence to consider, exemptions/waivers, valuation of benefits, and public charge bond rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien’s credit history and credit score
rubrics_metrics.description: The alien’s credit history and credit score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the factors DHS will consider in determining likelihood of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private health insurance or financial resources for foreseeable medical costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the alien has private health insurance or the financial resources to pay for reasonably foreseeable medical costs related to a medical condition that is likely to require extensive medical treatment or institutionalization or that will interfere with the alien’s ability to provide care for him- or herself, to attend school, or to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a factor in public charge determinations; appears in both the general factors list and in the 'heavily weighed negative factors' when a diagnosed condition exists and the alien is uninsured and lacks prospect of insurance or resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien’s education and skills (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard. When considering an alien’s education and skills, DHS will consider whether the alien has adequate education and skills to either obtain or maintain employment sufficient to avoid becoming a public charge, if authorized for employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS consideration includes (but is not limited to) the evidence items listed below. DHS will weigh the alien’s education and skills against likelihood of future self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills — evidence: history of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence item: The alien’s history of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as an example of evidence DHS may consider when assessing education and skills for public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills — evidence: educational attainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence item: Whether the alien has a high school degree (or its equivalent) or higher education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as an example of evidence DHS may consider when assessing education and skills for public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills — evidence: occupational skills/certifications/licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence item: Whether the alien has any occupational skills, certifications, or licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as an example of evidence DHS may consider when assessing education and skills for public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills — evidence: language proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence item: Whether the alien is proficient in English or proficient in other languages in addition to English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language proficiency is listed as relevant evidence for assessing ability to obtain/maintain employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective immigration status and expected period of admission (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard. The immigration status that the alien seeks and the expected period of admission as it relates to the alien’s ability to financially support for himself or herself during the duration of their stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will consider whether the alien is applying for adjustment of status or admission in a nonimmigrant or immigrant classification, and, for nonimmigrants, the classification and anticipated period of temporary stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of support requirement (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficient affidavit of support, when required under section 212(a)(4) of the Act, must meet the sponsorship and income requirements of section 213A of the Act and comply with 8 CFR 213a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will consider evidence including the sponsor’s annual income, assets, and resources; the sponsor's relationship to the applicant; and the likelihood that the sponsor would actually provide the statutorily-required amount of financial support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavily weighed negative factors (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following factors will generally weigh heavily in favor of a finding that an alien is likely to become a public charge. The mere presence of any one enumerated circumstance is not, alone, determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of heavily weighed negative factors (see guidance field). DHS treats these factors as generally having heavy weight in inadmissibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavily weighed negative factors — enumerated items
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated heavily weighed negative factors: (i) not a full-time student, authorized to work, but unable to demonstrate current employment, recent employment history or no reasonable prospect of future employment; (ii) currently receiving or certified/approved to receive one or more public benefits (as defined in 212.21(b)); (iii) received one or more public benefits within the 36 months immediately preceding the application; (iv) diagnosed with a medical condition likely to require extensive treatment/institutionalization or interfere with self-care/education/work AND uninsured with neither prospect of obtaining private insurance nor financial resources to pay for foreseeable medical costs; (v) previously been found inadmissible or deportable on public charge grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each listed circumstance will generally weigh heavily toward a public charge finding, though no single circumstance is automatically determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavily weighed positive factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The following factors will generally weigh heavily in favor of a finding that an alien is not likely to become a public charge: (i) household has financial assets/resources/support of at least 250 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for household size; (ii) authorized to work and currently employed with annual income of at least 250 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for household size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thresholds are singled out as heavily weighted positive indicators of self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of benefits received before specified cutoff date
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of this regulation, DHS will consider as a negative factor any amount of cash assistance for income maintenance (including SSI, TANF, State and local cash assistance 'General Assistance', and programs (including Medicaid) supporting aliens institutionalized for long-term care) received, or certified for receipt, before [INSERT DATE 60 DAYS FROM DATE OF PUBLICATION OF THE FINAL RULE], as provided under the 1999 Interim Field Guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS does not consider any other public benefits received or certified for receipt before such date. This paragraph identifies which pre-cutoff benefits DHS will treat as a negative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutorily or regulatorily exempt categories include (but are not limited to) refugees at admission and adjustment, asylees at grant and adjustment, Amerasian immigrants under specified law, Afghan and Iraqi interpreters and certain national employees, Cuban and Haitian entrants under specified statutes, certain NACARA and Haitian Refugee adjustments, Lautenberg parolees, special immigrant juveniles, registry applicants, TPS applicants/re-registrants, multiple specified nonimmigrant diplomats/government officials/NATO categories, T and U nonimmigrants and applicants adjusting under certain provisions, VAWA self-petitioners, qualified aliens under PRWORA Section 431(c), applicants under certain NDAA/National Defense statutes, American Indians born in Canada under section 289, Texas Band of Kickapoo Indians, nationals adjusting under specific public laws, Polish and Hungarian parolees, and any other categories exempt under law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhaustive list of statutory/regulatory exemptions is provided in § 212.23(a). Exemptions are based on specific statutory authorities and references to the Act and other public laws and CFR provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waivers of public charge inadmissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A waiver for the public charge ground of inadmissibility may be authorized based on statutory or regulatory authority for specified categories, including certain T and S nonimmigrant cases and other waivers authorized under law or regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: § 212.23(b) lists categories for which waivers may be authorized (e.g., nonimmigrants admitted under 101(a)(15)(T) applying for adjustment under 245(l)(2)(A); applicants under 101(a)(15)(S); certain S nonimmigrants applying for adjustment under 245(j); and any other waiver authorized by law or regulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation of monetizable benefits — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the cumulative value of one or more monetizable benefits listed in 8 CFR 212.21(b)(1)(ii) for public charge determinations, DHS will rely on benefit-specific methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation prescribes benefit-specific calculation methods for SNAP, Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance, and household cash benefits; DHS will calculate the value attributable to the alien in proportion to the number of people covered and based on amounts received within applicable 12-consecutive-month periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation method for SNAP
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to SNAP, DHS will calculate the value of the benefit attributable to the alien in proportion to the total number of people covered by the benefit, based on the amount(s) deposited within the applicable period of 12 consecutive months in which the benefits are received in the Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) card account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses EBT deposit amounts over a 12-month window and apportions benefit value to the alien by household share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation method for Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to Section 8 Housing Assistance (Housing Choice Voucher), DHS will calculate the value of the voucher attributable to the alien in proportion to the total number of people covered by the benefit, based on amounts within the applicable 12-consecutive-month period in which the benefits are received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS apportions voucher value by household coverage over a 12-month period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation method for Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: For Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance (including Moderate Rehabilitation), DHS will calculate the value of the rental assistance attributable to the alien in proportion to the total number of people covered by the benefit, based on the amount(s) received within the applicable 12 consecutive months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS apportions project-based rental assistance value by household share across a 12-month window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuation method for household cash benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to any cash benefit received by the alien on a household (rather than individual) basis, DHS will calculate the value of the benefit attributable to the alien in proportion to the total number of people covered by the benefit, based on the amounts received within the applicable period of 12 consecutive months in which the benefit is received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household-level cash benefits are prorated to the alien by household size using a 12-month receipt window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond — discretionary allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: After an alien has been found inadmissible as likely to become a public charge, DHS may allow the alien to submit a public charge bond if the alien is otherwise admissible; the decision is in DHS’s discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an alien has one or more heavily weighed negative factors as defined in 8 CFR 212.22, DHS generally will not favorably exercise discretion to allow submission of a public charge bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and execution requirements for public charge bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may require a surety bond, or cash or any cash equivalent (as listed in 8 CFR 103.6) and associated agreements to secure a bond. All bonds and agreements must be executed on a form designated by DHS and in accordance with form instructions; surety bonds must comply with 8 CFR 103.6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cash or cash equivalent secures a bond, DHS must issue a receipt on a DHS-designated form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of public charge bond
rubrics_metrics.description: Any public charge bond (or agreements to secure it) must be in an amount decided by DHS, not less than $10,000, annually adjusted for inflation based on CPI‑U, and rounded up to the nearest dollar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bond amount may not be appealed by the alien or the obligor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and duration of public charge bond
rubrics_metrics.description: A public charge bond must remain in effect until the alien naturalizes or otherwise obtains U.S. citizenship, permanently departs the United States, or dies; or the alien requests cancellation after 5 years as an LPR; or the alien changes to a status not subject to public charge inadmissibility and the bond is cancelled in accordance with the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An alien on whose behalf a bond has been submitted may not receive any public benefits (as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b)) after adjustment of status to lawful permanent resident until the bond is cancelled. Aliens must comply with any other bond conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission and notification requirements for bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: A public charge bond may be submitted only after DHS notifies the alien (and representative) that a bond may be submitted; the bond must be submitted per the DHS-designated form, with the fee prescribed in 8 CFR 103.7(b), and any procedures in the DHS notification. DHS will specify amount, duration, and other conditions and will notify the alien and representative when the bond is accepted and provide copies of communications between obligor and government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligor must notify DHS within 30 days of any change in physical or mailing address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution process for public charge bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bond not eligible for cancellation must be substituted prior to expiration, either the previous obligor or a new obligor may submit a substitute bond. Timelines and requirements differ based on whether the prior bond had a date-certain expiration or was unlimited; substitute bond must meet all initial bond requirements and new obligor assumes all liabilities and must cover breaches that occurred before DHS accepted the substitute bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS reviews substitute bond for sufficiency, will cancel previous bond and replace if substitute is sufficient; DHS will notify obligor to correct deficiencies within a timeframe; if not corrected and prior bond still in effect, prior bond remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation of public charge bond — grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien or obligor may request bond cancellation if the alien: (i) naturalized or otherwise obtained U.S. citizenship; (ii) permanently departed the U.S.; (iii) died; (iv) reached 5-year anniversary since becoming an LPR; or (v) obtained a different immigration status not subject to public charge inadmissibility following grant of LPR status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent departure is defined (loss/abandonment of LPR status plus physical departure) and voluntary loss requires submission of a record of abandonment form. Cancellation must be requested on DHS form with fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation process and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The alien and obligor have the burden to establish, by a preponderance of the evidence, that a cancellation condition has been met. If DHS finds information insufficient, it may request additional information per 8 CFR 103.2(b)(8). DHS must cancel a bond if it determines conditions have been met and the bond was not breached; for 5-year cancellations the alien/obligor must establish the bond was not breached during the 5-year period preceding the fifth anniversary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will notify obligor, alien, and representative of decision. When cancelled, the obligor is released; cash deposits are refunded. If DHS denies cancellation, it will notify reasons and the obligor’s right to appeal under 8 CFR part 103, subpart A. The alien and the alien’s representative may not appeal a denial to cancel or file a motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of bond breach and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond is breached if the alien has received public benefits (as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b)) after adjustment to LPR and before bond cancellation, or if other bond conditions imposed by DHS are otherwise breached. Benefits received while the alien is in an exempt category under 8 CFR 212.23 following initial grant of LPR, or benefits received after citizenship, may not be considered in breach determinations. DHS will not consider certain benefits received by enlisted servicemembers (or spouse/child) under specified 10 U.S.C. provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation clarifies exclusions and special rules for breach determinations (exempt categories, citizenship, military service).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach adjudication procedures, notice, and opportunity to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will determine whether bond conditions have been breached. If DHS lacks sufficient information from the benefit granting agency or the alien/obligor, it may request additional information. If DHS intends to declare a breach based on information not protected from disclosure to the obligor, it will disclose such information to the obligor to the extent permitted by law and provide an opportunity to respond and submit rebuttal evidence within a specified deadline; DHS will send a copy to the alien and representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After obligor's response or expiration of the deadline, DHS makes a breach determination and notifies obligor, alien, and representative. If DHS determines breach, obligor has right to appeal under 8 CFR part 103, subpart A; alien and representative may not appeal or file a motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of breach: claims, demand for payment, and amount
rubrics_metrics.description: An administratively final determination that a bond has been breached creates a claim in favor of the United States that may not be released or discharged by an immigration officer. Demands for amounts due under the bond are sent to the obligor or agent/co-obligor after declaration of breach becomes administratively final. The bond must be considered breached in the full amount of the bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A breach determination is administratively final when the time to file an appeal has expired or appeal is dismissed/rejected. Exhaustion of administrative remedies applies: a party has not exhausted remedies until a final administrative decision under 8 CFR part 103, subpart A is obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonimmigrant extension/change of status — benefit receipt requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where the nonimmigrant classification is exempt from section 212(a)(4) or that section has been waived, as a condition for approval of extension of status or change of nonimmigrant classification, the alien must demonstrate that he or she has not received since obtaining the nonimmigrant status for which he or she seeks to extend (or change), is not currently receiving, nor is likely to receive, a public benefit as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b). DHS will consider benefits received on or after [INSERT DATE 60 DAYS FROM DATE OF PUBLICATION OF THE FINAL RULE].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing whether the alien has met the burden, DHS will consider the nonimmigrant classification sought, reasons for extension/change, and expected period of stay. DHS may require submission of a declaration of self-sufficiency on a DHS-designated form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of self-sufficiency documentary requirement for adjustment of status
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of public charge determinations under section 212(a)(4) and 8 CFR 212.22, an alien seeking adjustment of status under Part 245 must submit a declaration of self-sufficiency on a form designated by DHS, in accordance with form instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit documentary requirement added to § 245.4(b); DHS may use the declaration as part of the public charge assessment.
